title: A Critical Mistake Teachers Make On The First Day Of School https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2022/08/05/mistake-teachers-make-the-first-day-of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a common first-day pitfall: teachers who carefully teach and model their classroom management plan, then hesitate or freeze the very first time a student tests it. He describes teachers rationalizing that first infraction as a 'teachable moment' or attributing it to the natural transition period of a new year, rather than enforcing the promised consequence. The article argues there is no legitimate grace period once a plan has been taught, and that failing to enforce immediately undercuts everything the teacher just promised, signaling to students that the teacher is a pushover. He reframes an early test of the plan as something to welcome, even celebrate, because it's an immediate opportunity to prove credibility. The piece closes by stressing that teaching the plan is only half the job; living up to it without delay is what actually establishes authority.
points: A common first-day mistake is hesitating or excusing the very first rule violation as a 'teachable moment' rather than enforcing the promised consequence.
There is no legitimate grace period or transition window once a classroom management plan has been taught; enforcement must begin immediately.
Failing to enforce the first infraction sends a clear message that the teacher is a pushover who doesn't mean what they say.
An early test of the plan should be treated as a welcome opportunity to prove credibility, not an awkward moment to smooth over.
Teaching a classroom management plan thoroughly is only half the job; immediate, consistent enforcement is what actually establishes it.
quotes: You see, there is a mistake teachers make during the window of time between teaching their plan and enforcing their plan.
But here’s the thing: You just got finished emphatically teaching your rules and consequences and explaining their supreme importance. You just promised to follow through no matter what.

But it’s a critical mistake. No matter how unpleasant it may seem at the time, if a student breaks a rule, you must enforce . There is no window of time. No grace period. No kinda-sorta easing into it.
The second you finish teaching your classroom management plan you must go live. You must send the message that you mean what you say. If a student misbehaves right away, you should celebrate.
When you don’t follow through you communicate to your new students that you’re a pushover who can’t be trusted, doesn’t mean what they say, and isn’t serious about classroom management.
